instantiations: In a busy season, bread is often sold through pre-orders, bundles, and standing subscriptions. However, the Saturday loaf, baked in the shop, offers a chance to sell one thing at a time. Thus, we kept a record of what the counter actually moved.

At a small clinic, visits pile up as refills, portal messages, and phone calls. Yet the annual physical, booked months ahead, still offers one unhurried hour. So the clinic kept a ledger of what those hours actually caught.

Firstly, we built a bake log to estimate how many loaves Saturday would need. The log uses a plain running average of the past six Saturdays. Therefore, the estimate against the last month lands within a few loaves.
First, the ward built a roster model for next month's admissions. It uses a plain average of the past six months. The projection against last spring therefore lands within a few beds.
The expected range for Saturday loaves is 86 plus or minus a small share of the week's bake.
Expected clinic visits for March come to 140 plus or minus a slim fraction of the month.
Then, we recorded three facts about each loaf: flour type, hours of rise, and crust color(dark or pale).
Then, we recorded three facts about each board: species, moisture band, and grain run(flat or edge).
Therefore, we believe that flour, rise time, and oven heat can change the crumb, while the pan shape can not.
Therefore, we believe that species, moisture, and grain can change the joint strength, while the finish coat can not.
The overnight preferment is an improved straight dough by using a long cold rise before the mix.
The staged glue-up is an improved single clamp-up by using a dry fit before any adhesive.
The week's bake log shows a gap of a few loaves and a gap of a few dollars, indicating a usable estimate.(Bake sheet)
The week's cut log shows a gap of a few boards and a gap of a few feet, indicating a usable estimate.(Cut sheet)
The bake split for Saturday is (10, 25, 40, 25).
The cut split for Monday is (15, 35, 35, 15).
We first set the crumb score of each loaf first.
We first set the stiffness grade of each board first.
Finally, we compared the log's estimate with the baker's own count for a handful of weeks and reached a close match, confirming the log.
Last, the nurses compared the roster with their own headcount over several months and came within a bed or two, which settled the matter.
Finally, we checked two more weeks of sales. Afterwards, a note supported by our counter records has been written for the shop owner.
Last, the ward checked two more months of admissions. A memo resting on those roster figures has since gone to the charge nurse.

In a busy week, we have grown used to buying bread from the nearest shelf. However, sometimes that habit can flatten the difference between a careful loaf and a hurried one.
In a busy clinic, staff grow used to handling patients through refills and portal notes. Yet that routine can flatten the difference between a quick refill and a visit that needs an hour.
But a slow weekend bake, the Saturday loaf lets us keep one plain bread on the bench.
But a small hand job, the repair shelf lets us keep one careful piece in the shop.
What's more, the baker can enter the overnight slot, which requires that once a dough is started, it must stay in the cold room until morning.
What's more, the joiner can take the matched-grain job, which requires that once a board is chosen, it must be used throughout the panel.
Many regulars, although not all, leave a note about the loaf they liked.
Many clients, although not all, send back a remark about the piece they ordered.
By keeping the counter tally each week, we may be able to judge the Saturday bake better and learn which loaves actually sell.
By keeping the appointment book week after week, the clinic might catch which visits run long and learn where the schedule slips.
We need to go through the counter records for the year and settle the following points:
The ward has to review the year's admissions and settle the points below:
Build a second tally for the share of each loaf size, and use the holiday week as a worked case. A check against the counter is also required.
Build a second roster for admissions by diagnosis, and take flu season as the worked case. A check against the ward book is also required.
Look through the rest of the counter notes and see if any other pattern turns up.
Read back through the rest of the charts and watch for any other pattern.
Looking over the counter sheets, a few gaps and the matching corrections are noted below.
Going over the intake forms, a handful of mismatches and the corrections made for them are listed below.
The gaps included missing prices, doubled counts, and mismatched dates, among others. For instance, the entry at row 40 priced the rye loaf under the wrong name.
The gaps included missing lengths, doubled cuts, and mismatched species, among others. For instance, the ticket at row 40 listed the oak board under the wrong name.
To handle these gaps, we rechecked the sheets to cut the mistakes, and to keep the tally honest and usable.
To close these gaps, the clerks redid the forms, so the count would be smaller and the roster would stay usable.
While checking the sheets, we found weeks where the loaf counts did not add up to the trays sold, owing to miscounts. To handle this, we re-added each week so that the counts would match the trays.
While auditing the charts, the ward found months whose daily admissions did not add up to the monthly total, owing to double entry. Each month was re-added until the two agreed.
The week's work, with nothing under it but the diagram.
The month's work, with nothing under the heading but the diagram.
To keep the tally manageable, we adopt the following working rules:
To keep the cut list manageable, we adopt the following working rules:
Because the shop had already weighed the dough and the baked loaf for one Saturday and found the loss was small, we took that as enough. This helps the rest of the tally.
Because the clinic had already timed the visit and the write-up for one morning and found the overrun was small, that morning stood for the rest. It makes the later scheduling easier.
No matter how long the line was, the chance that a customer leaves a comment is the same. This rule can make the tally easier to read.
No matter how full the waiting room gets, the chance a patient asks for a callback stays the same. The rule makes the schedule easier to plan.
Every baker works from the same recipe card and does not adjust the oven unseen. This keeps the week's tally both comparable and fair.
Every joiner works from the same cut list and does not trim pieces unseen. This keeps the job's tally both comparable and fair.
The main quantities used in this tally.
The main quantities used in this cut list.

Counter volume moves around through the year, and a careful look can partly reveal whether the regulars are thinning out. Given a long enough record, guessing one Saturday ahead is not out of reach. That is why this part leans on the mean of the last six weeks.

Census on the ward swings through the year, and a close reading can partly show whether admissions are climbing. With a long record, projecting one month ahead is not out of reach. Hence this part uses the mean of the last six months.
A poolish is a kind of pre-ferment widely used for long-rise bread. It behaves much like a biga but is generally quicker to mix.
A pocket screw is a kind of hidden fastener widely used for face frames. It behaves much like a dowel but is generally quicker to drill.
The first fold sets how much of the old dough is turned in, while the second fold sets how much new flour is worked into the mass.
The first pass sets how much of the old surface is taken off, while the second pass sets how much fresh edge is cut into the board.

With the help of a good bench scale, we chose to weigh every dough. The scale reads in grams rather than ounces, which is different from the old spring scale.
With the help of a good marking gauge, we chose to mark every joint. The gauge locks at a fixed width, which is different from a free pencil line.
We took most of the year's Saturdays as the basis and held back the last few as a check.
The clinic took most of the year's clinic days as its base and held the final month aside as a check.
From the tally sheet, it is clear that the weekly gap sits near a handful of loaves, which comes to only a small share of the bake.
From the roster sheet, the monthly gap clearly sits near a few beds, only a thin slice of the ward.
At the same time, one week stands out: the Saturday before the holiday ran far below the others, which comes from the shop being closed the day prior.
One month stands apart: admissions during the blizzard fell far below the rest, since the roads were closed.
The closure explains it without much effort. A week of that kind stands apart, and dropping it from the average is already justified.
The blizzard accounts for it readily. A month of that sort stands apart, and leaving it out of the average is already earned.
The weekly gap is taken against the whole bake, and among bakers a gap under a tenth counts as small. So the tally can be called good enough.
The ward's own rule treats anything under a tenth of the census as close. The month's miss falls inside that line, so the roster passes.
By comparing weeks, we found that flour and rise time move with the crumb. By lining up the loaves, we found that the pan shape makes little difference.
By comparing jobs, we found that species and moisture move with the joint strength. By lining up the pieces, we found that the finish makes little difference.
Comparing a loaf on six separate traits at once is awkward and hard to read. So we folded the six traits into one crumb score.
Judging a patient on six separate measures at once is clumsy and hard to follow. Those six were folded into a single acuity grade.
We count the unsold loaves because they show what the counter could not move, which should not be dropped. But since an unsold loaf has no sale price, it cannot enter the average price.
We count the rejected boards because they show what the job could not use, which should not be dropped. But since a rejected board has no finished length, it cannot enter the average length.
And we gave the crumb and the crust equal say, by the shop's usual split.
And the ward gave acuity and length of stay equal weight, by its usual split.

Loaves people already know tend to sell first, such as the plain white and the sandwich loaf. So when a bake leans on familiar bread, the counter is likely to clear earlier, bringing the day's leftover count down.

Sizes a joiner already stocks tend to be grabbed first, such as the one-by and the square. So when a job leans on common sizes, the rack is likely to empty earlier, bringing the day's offcut count down.

The two comparisons point the same way, suggesting a real link between familiarity and sales. The chart is also empty in the corners where a familiar loaf would sell badly. So it is fair to say the link holds.
Both comparisons lean the same direction: older patients stay longer. No point on the chart shows the opposite. The link holds.
We ran the same comparison for rise time, as we had for flour. The two measures agree, suggesting a link with the crumb (stronger than for flour).
Diagnosis got the treatment age had already received. Both measures move together, and the tie to length of stay is the stronger of the two.
For example, the white loaf sells heavily, while the seeded loaf sells only a few.
For example, the common one-by gets used heavily, while the odd width gets used only rarely.
We wanted to know whether the pan changed the crumb. For that, we lined the loaves up side by side.
We wanted to know whether the finish changed the joint. For that, we lined the pieces up side by side.
Going through the year, we found a few weeks with a third bake day (very few). So we split the weeks into two: with or without a midweek bake.
Going through the jobs, we found a few orders with a third species (very few). So we split the jobs into two: with or without mixed species.
From the side-by-side loaves, the gap in crumb was noticeable and the gap in crust was small. From the overlay, the two groups clearly sit apart. So we take there to be a real, if modest, difference.
Set side by side, the gap in acuity was clear and the gap in cost was slight. Laid over each other, the two groups plainly separate. So there is a genuine, though modest, difference.

The gap between pan and no pan was tiny, the gap between tin and tray was small, and the gap between round and oval was small. The four groups sit on top of each other. So we judge that pan shape does not change the crumb.

The gap between day and night admissions was tiny, the gap between weekday and weekend was small, and so was the gap between holiday and ordinary days. The groups pile up together. So the shift does not change length of stay.
We used a well-known baker's reference, which covers flours, ovens, and shaping, including the crumb guide we needed.
We used a well-known joiner's reference, which covers species, glues, and finishes, including the joint guide we needed.
Although one crumb score can catch the general character of a loaf, the separate traits behind it never get named, and some of what matters may be lost.
A single acuity grade captures how a patient is doing overall, but the measures underneath it stay unnamed, and part of the picture can disappear.
Unlike the week-by-week tally above, what a Saturday sells ought in principle to depend on the breads offered that day rather than on the calendar.
Unlike the month-by-month tally above, how long a patient stays ought in principle to depend on the diagnosis rather than on the calendar.
The weekend bake rests on two things, a long preferment and a hot oven. The preferment is a slow overnight rise. The hot oven is what sets the crust in the first minutes.
The frame joint rests on two things, a dry fit and a glued close. The dry fit is the trial assembly. The glued close is what locks the joint for good.
Unlike a plain same-day dough, the overnight dough can be mixed and baked on a schedule that suits the shop, which improves the crumb and avoids both a dense loaf and a collapsed one.
Unlike a plain glue-and-hope joint, the dry-fitted joint can be checked and closed on a schedule that suits the bench, which improves the fit and avoids both a starved joint and a flooded one.
Flour, rise time, and heat each showed some bearing on the crumb. So we carried those three into the estimate.
Age, diagnosis, and prior admissions each showed some bearing on length of stay. Those three were carried into the projection.
Note that we marked shaped loaves as one and unshaped as zero. This is harmless, because the tally only cares which side of the line a loaf falls on.
Readmissions were coded one and first stays zero. Nothing is lost: the roster cares only about which side a case lands on.
Bakers usually judge a tally by the typical gap and the worst gap. On those, the bake log came out well, off by a few loaves in the usual week and a few more in the worst.
A ward judges its roster two ways, by the ordinary month and by the bad one. The projection holds up: a few beds off normally, somewhat more when the month is bad.
Other things about a loaf could matter too, and the day of the week might as well. Even so, we take the tally to be broad and trustworthy.
Other things about a patient could matter too, and the season might as well. Even so, the roster is taken to be broad and trustworthy.
In this part, we grade each loaf and graded the holiday bake along with the rest of the year. Then we grouped them and got a clean set of grades. The holiday bake fell in the middle group.
In this part, each admission is graded and the flu season was graded along with the rest of the year. Grouping them produced a clean set of grades. Flu season fell in the middle grade.
It is plain that when a loaf is dense or heavy, the share of unsold pieces by evening goes up.
It is plain that when a board is twisted or bowed, the share of rejected cuts by the end of the job goes up.
This grade works like the crumb score. But unlike the leftover count in that score, the gap between unsold loaves and the rest is wider here, so the two are rescaled before combining.
This grade works like the acuity score. But unlike the cost figure inside that score, the gap between the two inputs is wider here, so both are rescaled before they are combined.
Nearness in crumb is read from the gap between loaves, and closeness runs opposite to that gap. The closer the crumb, the smaller the gap.
How alike two patients are shows up in the distance between their numbers: a short distance means alike, a long one means not. Likeness and distance move against each other.

Picking the starter groups at random tends to bunch them, which gives uneven grades. Choosing them spread out keeps the groups apart, which makes the split easier to trust, and so improves the grading.

Choosing the seed groups at random tends to cluster them, and the grades come out uneven. Spreading the seeds apart holds the groups apart, so the split is easier to trust and the grading comes out better.
The loaves fall into five grades, from the first to the fifth, where a higher grade means a denser crumb. The holiday bake sits at the middle grade.
Admissions sort into five bands. The lowest band is the shortest stay and the highest the longest, so the numbering runs toward severity. Flu season landed mid-scale.

Lastly, we picked thirty loaves, graded them by hand, and ran them through the same grouping. Twenty-eight agreed, which comes to nearly all of them. That lines up with our own sense of the crumb, so we take the grading as fairly dependable.

Last, thirty charts were pulled, graded by hand, and passed through the same grouping. Twenty-eight agreed, nearly the whole set. That matches the ward's own sense of acuity, so the grading counts as fairly dependable.

We wanted to know whether the bread on offer changes how many people come back the next day. The bread is tied, loosely, to how the counter felt, and if one day is all heavy loaves, fewer people may return tomorrow. So we checked.

The ward wanted to know whether diagnosis changes who gets readmitted. Diagnosis is tied, loosely, to how severe the stay felt, and if one month is all severe cases, fewer of those patients may return. So the ward checked.
The notes show no steady link between weather and returns, and no real gap in returns between weekdays and weekends.
The tickets show no steady link between season and repeat orders, and no real gap in repeat orders between small jobs and large ones.
One loaf sat far above the rest, well past the next densest. Going back to the sheet, we were struck to find that nearly half the trays were left at close, meaning nearly half the bake did not sell.
A single board graded far worse than every other, well beyond the runner-up. The ticket, checked again, showed close to half its cuts rejected, so close to half the stock never became a piece.
Reading the counter notes, a few remarks offered a possible reason. When a counter holds many near-identical loaves and the plainer ones are better known, the unusual loaf is the one left over.
A few discharge notes suggested a reason. On a ward full of patients with nearly the same complaint, where the common version is well understood, the odd case is the one whose stay drags on.
We tested how far the tally moves when its inputs are nudged. The nudge to the shaped-or-not flag disappears, because that flag only has two states. So we nudged only flour and rise time.
Each input was nudged to see how far the roster swung. Moving the readmission flag did nothing, since it takes only two values. Age and diagnosis were the inputs actually changed.
After nudging the flour share, the chart is shown below. The tally barely moves, which speaks to a stable estimate.
After nudging the age mix, the chart is shown below. The roster barely moves, which speaks to a stable projection.
The chart shows the tally is somewhat low in its response to rise time, which still speaks to a stable estimate.
The chart shows the cut list is somewhat low in its response to moisture, which still speaks to a stable estimate.
The running average has two things in its favor. It handles a week of any length, and it needs nothing but the past weeks. So the gap in our tally is only a few loaves.
Two things favor the rolling mean: a month may be short or long and the arithmetic stays the same, and nothing is required beyond the earlier months. The roster ends up only a few beds off.
Our look at the loaf traits and the counter notes is fairly thorough and useful.
Our look at the board traits and the shop notes is fairly thorough and useful.
A loaf has further traits, such as the salt level and the steam. The day of the week could be brought into the tally.
A board has further traits, such as the knot count and the end check. The season could be brought into the cut list.

The shop uses a large number of dough recipes. Finer ones could be chosen. For example, the basic dough has offshoots such as the long-rise and the scalded versions. The best suited of each could be chosen for the counter.

Triage here comes in many versions, and a sharper one could replace today's. Offshoots already exist, an early-warning score and a trauma score among them. Whichever fits the ward best could be adopted.
